questions.question: Define potential energy and describe three kinds, each with two examples.
questions.expected_answer: Potential energy is stored energy that an object or substance has because of its position, condition or chemical make-up. Gravitational potential energy: stored in raised objects, such as water behind a dam, a rock at the top of a cliff, a learner at the top of a slide. Elastic potential energy: stored in stretched, squashed or bent objects, such as a stretched catapult, a drawn bow, a compressed spring. Chemical potential energy: stored in substances and released by reactions, such as food, fuels (coal, petrol, wood), batteries, matches.

questions.question: Explain why food is a store of energy, how food energy is shown on labels, and why fatty foods contain more energy.
questions.expected_answer: Plants capture the Sun's energy in photosynthesis and store it as chemical potential energy in sugars, starch, fats and proteins; our cells release it by respiration. Labels show energy in kilojoules per serving and per 100 g or 100 ml. Fats store about 37 kJ per gram, more than twice as much as carbohydrates or proteins (about 17 kJ per gram), so fatty foods are energy-dense.

questions.question: Define kinetic energy, name the two factors it depends on, and describe the energy changes of a child on a swing.
questions.expected_answer: Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving. It depends on speed (faster means more, strongly so) and mass (heavier means more). At the top of the swing the child is momentarily still, with no kinetic energy and the most gravitational potential energy. Swinging down, potential energy changes into kinetic energy and the child speeds up, with the most kinetic energy at the lowest point. Rising again, kinetic energy changes back into potential energy and the child slows down.
